doc.title: Lew Soloff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000

title: Manhattan Jazz Quintet and its success in Japan
summary: The MJQ's hit record in the mid-1980s, its many albums, and his frustration at keeping the formula.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Near the end, yeah. Of course. Because he didn’t want to bring something in and have it put down. And he was the real, amazing creative energy in that band. Actually so was Al Cooper, before I was there. I loved his songs. But it doesn’t matter. I’m always of the mind that if a band is allowed to just continuously try to be creative they’re better off than if they have a hit and they try to keep following that formula. I’m even of that mind with the Manhattan Jazz Quintet which I’m in, which you may have heard of or may not. It’s a band that’s extremely popular in Japan, a jazz quintet. We made a record in the early eighties, maybe ’84 or so. The record was projected to sell about 8,000 copies. Within several months it had sold well over 80,000 copies, and shortly after that it went up to about 160,000 copies. And when you’re talking about a country the size of Japan you multiply it by ten to imagine what it would be like in sales here. And for a jazz record, that’s a lot. Well now we’re making our 24th record as a quintet. We’ll be doing that in May or June. Our 24th record as a quintet. We just did our eighth outgrowth of the quintet, a big band album, the eighth one, so that’s 24, eight big band records, I did five solo records, give you $125 if you can find one — no, no. I did five solo records out of that, eight big band records, 24 quintet records, which will be shortly 24, a couple of orchestra records, all stemming out of this, plus many related projects with other artists that all came out of that for me. But the down side of it is that the band, which is on a level where it still works in Japan but not on that high level of hit that it was back in the late and mid eighties, they basically, and I’m not the leader, they basically are of the mind that we still have to follow the original formula of the band. And I think if we had just changed it radically we would be enjoying the music more and getting better critical approval. But I’m not the leader.

The format was originally and still is, at that time jazz was getting very, very avant garde in Japan and very out. And there was a feeling by some people that a group had to come together and play some of the straight ahead stuff made popular by some of the great groups like Horace Silver, Art Blakey, da- da- da- da- da, in a little bit of a different way.
